transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-16
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Meyers (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Reefline Head of Platform), Luis Ortega (Reefline SRE), Nina Park (Reefline CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Reefline evaluating Redwood for integrating LLM features across multi-tenant product. Main concerns: SDK/adapter compatibility with LangChain/LlamaIndex, gateway/proxy architecture to enforce per-tenant rate quotas, observability hooks and tracing, and security (VPC, KMS, SOC2). Discussed Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs and next steps for a pilot.

Topics: SDKs, LangChain/LlamaIndex adapters, gateway/proxy pattern, tenant rate limits/quotas, observability/tracing hooks, VPC/KMS, benchmarking/POC plan.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Meyers: hey everyone, thanks for taking time. i'm Jordan at Redwood, i'm the AE on this one. quick intros?
[00:07] Maya Chen: maya here, head of platform at reefline. we run the ingestion pipeline and the API gateway.
[00:12] Luis Ortega: luis, s-re, i handle infra and ops for our platform.
[00:16] Nina Park: nina, cto, i want to understand risk and runbooks.
[00:20] Priya Nair: hey all, priya from redwood, i'm the solutions engineer, will dig into the integration details with langchain/llamaindex and the proxy pattern.

[00:35] Jordan: goal for today - understand your current architecture, constraints, and success criteria so we can map hosted vs dedicated vs private. also to surface any immediate blockers for a pilot.

[01:02] Maya: high level — we have multi-tenant app, each tenant gets prompts and embeddings pipeline. currently using LangChain v0.1x in python and LlamaIndex for retrieval layer. we are looking to move from openai to a more cost-predictable infra.
[01:18] Maya: two big asks: 1) have a proxy in front so we can enforce per-tenant quotas/rate-limits at our edge, and 2) observability hooks so our platform teams can trace requests end-to-end.

[01:40] Luis: for quotas -- we need per-tenant token quotas and per-route concurrency caps. we also have burst policy needs for premium tenants. and we need a way to map our API keys to redwood requests for billing correlation.

[02:05] Priya: okay makes sense. we typically see two patterns: embed a lightweight gateway/proxy as a sidecar or use our SDK directly in your backends. the sidecar/proxy approach lets you mediate auth, enforce per-tenant quotas, and annotate requests for observability before forwarding to Redwood hosted or dedicated endpoints.

[02:42] Jordan: quick note on deployment modes — hosted is fastest (api keys, no infra), dedicated gives you reserved GPU capacity and predictable latency, and private gives you the control (VPC or on-prem) for strict compliance.

[03:05] Nina: what's the difference operationally between a dedicated pool and private? like if we need HSM-backed KMS for keys and audit controls?

[03:18] Priya: dedicated is still managed by Redwood in our environment but isolated capacity, you get SLA-backed latency, and we provide KMS integrations. private — we ship a control plane that can sit in your VPC or on-prem and you manage keys with your HSM/KMS fully. private is the best fit for HSM/HIPAA/audit isolation.

[03:46] Luis: and network wise, private can be peered or run over direct connect?
[03:50] Priya: yes, VPC peering or direct connect options are supported for private. for dedicated we can also set up private peering but the control plane remains in our cloud.

[04:05] Maya: returning to SDKs — we use python langchain; will we get a drop-in connector?
[04:12] Priya: we have first-class SDKs for python and node. for LangChain specifically we provide an example connector and a minimal adapter pattern; for LlamaIndex we have a sample retriever wrapper. i'll share a sandbox repo.

[04:36] Jordan: one practical item — customers often want streaming with chunked responses and the ability to cancel. we support streaming and server-sent events, also streaming through the SDKs and webhooks for completions.

[05:00] Maya: great. about observability: can we get tracing headers through? we want to tie Redwood tokens to our distributed trace (jaeger/tempo) and have per-call cost metrics.

[05:14] Priya: yes — you can pass X-Request-ID and traceparent headers. we emit trace spans into our telemetry and can propagate your trace id through the request. on the console side you get token-level cost slices per request and per-route latency breakdowns.

[05:38] Luis: are there webhooks for eventing? e.g., if a model fails or we hit degraded capacity, we want alerts pushed into our oncall tooling.

[05:46] Priya: we support webhooks for model events and system alerts; you can also configure rate-based triggers to notify when throttling happens.

[06:08] Maya: about rate limits — does Redwood support hierarchical quotas (global account, tenant, route)? we need tenant limits but also route-level restrictions (e.g., embeddings heavy vs chat-light).

[06:20] Priya: yes, hierarchical quotas are supported. you can set global, tenant, and route limits. we also support token-based quotas and concurrency caps. plus you can define burst windows for premium tiers.

[06:42] Luis: how does that work with a proxy? we want the proxy to reject early to save cost, not forward a request that will be throttled.

[06:52] Priya: the proxy can call a local sync-check endpoint we provide or evaluate quota locally via a short TTL cache. for hosted we provide a quota-check API with low-latency response; for private/dedicated we can run quota evaluation next to your edge for near-zero RTT.

[07:20] Jordan: note — caching prefix keys and K-V cache of context helps reduce token volume for repeated prompts, which affects quota consumption.

[07:30] Maya: is that automatic? curious if that will break our prompt routing.

[07:36] Priya: we have automatic prefix caching for repeated prompts and optional KV cache controls you can tune. it's safe for retrieval-augmented flows but we give you hooks to invalidate cache per-tenant or per-conversation.

[08:02] Nina: security question — we need SOC2 plus an option for customer-managed encryption keys. do you support that?

[08:10] Priya: yes SOC2 is standard, we also support BYOK via KMS/HSM for private deployments and limited BYOK for dedicated via customer-managed keys integrated through our KMS partner flows. we'll send the security pack.

[08:36] Luis: one critical ops ask — in a failover scenario if the dedicated pool is down, can we fallback to hosted and maintain token routing? how does billing reconcile?

[08:50] Jordan: we do automated fallback policies. routing can be configured to fallback to a compatible model variant in hosted with a configurable grace policy. billing is tracked per-request; we'll surface the cost delta in the console and can emit events for reconciliations.

[09:20] Maya: let's talk about observability hooks in more detail — we want per-call metadata in our traces and the ability to export logs to our s3/elk stack.

[09:31] Priya: we push logs to customer destinations for private deployments, and for hosted/dedicated we support log export to S3 or a partner log forwarder; metrics get pushed to datadog/prometheus via sinks.

[09:50] Luis: what about token-level cost breakdown per request? that's key for our billing.

[09:56] Priya: console shows token breakdown, model used, execution time, and cost. there's also an exportable CSV/JSON per time range. you can attach your tenant id as a metadata field and we surface cost per tenant.

[10:18] Nina: we use LlamaIndex heavily for the retrieval side. are there concurrency limits on retrieval calls? some retrievals are low-latency but many parallel small ones.

[10:30] Priya: you can set concurrency caps per-route; also batching options can aggregate small retrieval requests internally to amortize cost if you opt in. for low-latency retrievals, we recommend a dedicated pool or private to avoid noisy neighbor effects.

[10:58] Maya: curious about SDK latency — what overhead do your SDKs introduce compared to raw HTTP calls?

[11:06] Priya: minimal — SDK adds request signing and convenience helpers. 10-30 ms typical overhead client-side; most latency is network + model runtime. for high-performance paths we recommend colocated private or dedicated in the same region.

[11:28] Luis: on instrumentation, do you provide sample OpenTelemetry spans?

[11:33] Priya: yes, we have OTEL examples for python and node, including span naming conventions, attributes we emit (model, tokens, latency, tenant_id).

[11:50] Jordan: let's do a quick architecture sketch — how is Reefline thinking of placing the proxy?

[11:56] Maya: we were thinking of an ingress proxy in the control plane: kube ingress auth layer that Enforces quotas and then forwards to our services which call Redwood. alternative was direct SDK calls from services with an internal middleware.

[12:12] Priya: both valid. ingress sidecar pattern centralizes enforcement but adds a hop. service-level SDKs simplify observability per request and reduce additional network hops. if you need early rejection to save cost, an ingress/proxy is better.

[12:35] Maya: cost tradeoff though — sidecar adds compute footprint.

[12:40] Jordan: but sidecar saves tokens by rejecting earlier and by consolidating cache. tradeoffs to model.

[12:52] Luis: on quotas again — can we enforce per-tenant contexts so that embeddings usage gets counted differently than chat usage? we want separate billing buckets.

[12:59] Priya: yes — route and model tagging allows separate quota and billing buckets. you can say route=embeddings has separate token bucket and higher per-token cost.

[13:20] Maya: any rough latency numbers for dedicated vs hosted?

[13:26] Priya: hosted typical p95 60-120ms for smaller context models; dedicated p95 can be 30-80ms depending on GPU size and config. private in-region colocation can hit sub-30ms for certain models.

[13:48] Luis: we need to run a spike test — we serve a few thousand concurrent small requests with seq length ~120 tokens. can we run a 48-hour test and measure tail latency and cost?

[13:59] Jordan: yes — we can provision a short-lived dedicated pool for the spike test or run a hosted stress test if you want to avoid a commit. we'll propose both approaches in the follow-up.

[14:20] Nina: compliance — we'll need contract language around data residency and deletion. does Redwood provide data deletion guarantees and audit logs?

[14:30] Priya: yes, we support data retention policies and deletion APIs; audit logs are available in the console and exported for private deployments. we'll include the deletion SLA in the security docs.

[14:48] Maya: a practical question — our developers use langchain's chains and indexers locally in notebooks. can they swap out the openai connector for a redwood connector without refactoring?

[15:00] Priya: in many cases yes. our langchain connector implements the standard LLM interface. for LlamaIndex our wrapper mimics the retriever API. there may be minor param naming diffs but we provide shim examples.

[15:18] Luis: billing mapping — we have internal tenant account id. can that be passed in per-request so chargebacks are automatic?

[15:26] Priya: yep, pass tenant metadata header, we'll persist it in logs and in the cost exports so you can reconcile.

[15:38] Maya: ok sounds good. another concern — model rollouts. we want to test a smaller model first, then push to larger for premium tenants. does Redwood support targetted rollouts?

[15:49] Jordan: yes canary and traffic splitting is built into rollouts. you can target by tenant id or route and set automatic fallback on quality regressions.

[16:05] Nina: are there guardrails for hallucination monitoring? any built-in evals?

[16:12] Priya: we have Redwood Optimize that can run prompt-based evals and quality monitors against a labeled set and raise regression alerts when metrics drift. we'll demo that in the POC if you'd like.

[16:28] Luis: what about rate-limit error semantics? we want 429 with a retry-after header ideally.

[16:34] Priya: yes 429 + Retry-After is standard, and we also emit error codes for quota vs concurrency vs model unavailable so you can take different client-side actions.

[16:52] Maya: curious about persistent connections and keepalive — important for our mobile clients.

[16:58] Priya: SDK supports HTTP keepalive and we can support long-lived HTTP/2 streams for streaming output. websocket is available too.

[17:15] Jordan: i'm going to surface some common POC patterns — usually we provide a sandbox api key + short dedicated pool for load tests, a sample langchain adapter, and a shared dashboard with tracing/metrics.

[17:30] Maya: good. on CSP and data residency — we operate in eu-west-1 region for europe tenants. can we pin region?

[17:38] Priya: yes region pinning is supported for models and endpoints; private obviously lets you fully control region and residency.

[17:52] Nina: question about license/usage — if we use open models does Redwood host model weights or do we bring our own?

[17:59] Priya: we host curated open models in our catalog and also support bringing your own model artifacts in private deployments. for dedicated we can host a customer model image in our infra under an agreed contract.

[18:18] Luis: telemetry — can we get per-tenant p95 and p99 and token histograms?

[18:25] Priya: yes per-tenant latency percentiles, token histograms, error rates, and we can export time series to your metrics backend.

[18:42] Maya: ok, what's the minimal set to unblock a POC?

[18:48] Jordan: minimal POC: sandbox keys, sample LangChain/LlamaIndex adapter, a short load test (hosted or temporary dedicated), and security docs. ideally we have tenant traffic profile and a tech contact.

[19:03] Maya: we'll provide traffic profile and a list of 5 test tenants.

[19:10] Luis: timeline — we aim to start POC this month and evaluate for production by end of q2. tight but possible.

[19:20] Jordan: noted. i'll follow up with pricing for a 2-week dedicated pilot and hosted-only options.

[19:30] Priya: i'll prepare the langchain shims and otel examples and a short runbook for the proxy sidecar pattern.

[19:38] Maya: on the quota enforcement, can you add an example snippet for how the proxy would consult the quota-check endpoint? that will help our engineers.

[19:46] Priya: yes i'll include a sample proxy middleware snippet (node and go).

[19:54] Nina: ok let's close with risks — mine are compliance docs timing, and cost predictability.

[19:59] Jordan: we will surface both in the follow-up: security pack + estimated cost model for your traffic.

[20:08] Luis: small nit — we've had bad experiences with connectors that change API shapes. please call out breaking changes policy.

[20:15] Priya: we have a versioning policy and deprecation windows; we'll include that in the docs and show the model & SDK version pins available.

[20:30] Maya: any competitors considerations? we evaluated openai because of familiarity and anthropic for safety profiles but wanted more deterministic economics than openai's variable pricing.

[20:45] Jordan: understood. Redwood is positioned for production economics and predictable serving; we'll include benchmarks that match your seq length.

[21:00] (crosstalk)
[21:12] Jordan: quick recap — action items, runbook, pricing, and security docs. proposed follow-up POC check-in on 2026-05-28.
[21:25] Maya: yep that works for us.
[21:30] Nina: thanks everyone.
[21:33] Jordan: thanks all, we'll follow up with the docs and a calendar invite.

[21:45] End of transcript.
